text: At the funeral Marcher stood among strangers, treated as no more than a distant acquaintance, for he possessed no recognized right to grieve for a woman who had been nothing to him in name. <break time="0.8s" /> Unable to bear the emptiness of London, he travelled for a long time in the East, but the wonders of Asia seemed dull to him compared with the one small grave he had left behind. <break time="0.8s" /> On his return he went to her grave again and again, where he would sit for hours on the cold stone, as if by staying near her he might recover some lost part of himself. <break time="0.8s" /> One autumn afternoon, at a fresh grave nearby, he saw a mourner whose face was so ravaged by grief that Marcher, as the man passed, felt as if he had been struck. <break time="0.8s" /> Never in his life had Marcher felt a passion like that, and he saw, with a terrible clearness, that the stranger had lived and loved, whereas he himself had merely waited. <break time="0.8s" /> The truth he had missed now stood before him in all its horror, namely that he was the man of his time to whom nothing on earth was ever to happen. <break time="0.8s" /> The escape would have been to love her, for then, and only then, would he have truly lived, and May, who had seen this long ago, had offered him that escape in vain. <break time="0.8s" /> At that moment he seemed to see the Beast at last, huge and hideous, rising for its long delayed leap, and to avoid it he flung himself face down upon her tomb.
